title: The Mystery of Roopkund
facts: Roopkund is a high‑altitude glacial lake in the Himalayas at 5,020 m (16,470 ft) elevation in Chamoli District, Uttarakhand, India.
The lake is seldom more than 40 m in diameter, covering about 1,000–1,500 m², and is about three metres deep.
Skeletons were rediscovered in 1942 by forest ranger Hari Kishan Madhwal of Nanda Devi National Park.
A National Geographic team retrieved about 30 skeletons in 2003, some still with flesh attached.
Radiocarbon dating at Oxford University placed the older group of remains at 850 CE ± 30 years (around 800 CE).

Genome‑wide analysis identified three distinct ancestry groups: 23 individuals (~800 CE) with South Asian ancestry, 1 individual (~1800 CE) with Southeast Asian ancestry, and 14 individuals (~1800 CE) with eastern Mediterranean ancestry.
The older South Asian remains appear to have been deposited over an extended period, while the younger Mediterranean and Southeast Asian remains were deposited in a single event.
Local legend attributes the deaths to a sudden hailstorm that killed a pilgrimage party led by King Raja Jasdhaval and his wife Rani Balampa.
The lake's skeletons are visible in clear water for about one month each year when the ice melts.
Tourists have been reported to remove bones on mules, prompting conservation concerns from Chamoli district authorities.
The lake freezes for most of the year; the optimal trekking season is autumn (mid‑September to October).
The typical multi‑day trek from Lohajung to Roopkund takes about five days and passes through alpine meadows such as Bedni Bugyal.
